title: Negotiation
in30Seconds: Negotiation is a discussion aimed at reaching an agreement — the back-and-forth that happens when two sides share some interests and oppose others. It shows up when salaries are offered, contracts are signed, conflicts are settled, and purchases are made. Skilled negotiators prepare a target and a walk-away point, look past positions to the interests underneath, and aim for a deal both sides can live with.
whyItMatters: Everyone negotiates something, most days: a start date, a price, a deadline, a share of the work. The stakes are rarely huge on any single day, but they compound — people who negotiate well keep more of what matters to them and, just as important, keep the relationships the deal depends on. Academically, negotiation is a named management competency: the U.S. Office of Personnel Management lists influencing and negotiating among the skills expected of senior federal leaders. Practically, the same preparation works at a salary talk or a farmers' market stall. And the mindset carries forward: knowing what you need and what the other side needs is a skill for life, not just for contracts.
learningObjectives: Define negotiation as a discussion aimed at reaching an agreement, attributing the working definition to Fisher, Ury, and Patton's Getting to Yes as presented by the Program on Negotiation.
Name four settings where negotiation happens — salaries, contracts, conflicts, and purchases — with an original example of each.
Distinguish positions, what each side says, from interests, what each side needs, using an original example.
Distinguish distributive negotiation, which divides a fixed pie, from integrative negotiation, which looks for ways to grow the pie.
Explain the preparation practice: know your target, your walk-away point, and the other side.
Apply the four-step process — open, explore, propose, agree — and the honest framing that the best deal is one both sides can live with.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition, attributed
collegeVersion.body: Negotiation is a discussion aimed at reaching an agreement. The working definition in this lesson comes from the Program on Negotiation at Harvard Law School, which quotes Roger Fisher, William Ury, and Bruce Patton's Getting to Yes: negotiation is back-and-forth communication designed to reach an agreement when you and the other side have some interests that are shared and others that are opposed. Corporate Finance Institute (CFI) agrees in plainer words: negotiation is a dialogue between two or more parties with the intention of reaching a mutually beneficial outcome or resolving a conflict. Two features of these definitions matter. First, negotiation is a discussion: people talk, trade, and adjust rather than command. Second, it is aimed at an agreement: both sides intend to end with a deal, not just with a lecture. The phrase some interests shared and others opposed is the heart of it — if every interest were shared, there would be nothing to negotiate, and if none were shared, there would be no reason to talk.

collegeVersion.heading: When negotiation happens
collegeVersion.body: Negotiation is everywhere people have to share something scarce: time, money, tasks, or rights. Salaries: a job offer is a starting point, not a final answer — an applicant and a hiring manager discuss pay and start dates until both accept the terms. Contracts: a bakery and a delivery company do not just sign the printed agreement; they talk through rates, routes, and late-delivery penalties first. Conflicts: when two departments both need the same conference room, someone has to negotiate the schedule rather than let the argument fester. Purchases: the sticker price on a used car is an invitation to talk, and buyer and seller go back and forth until they find a number both can accept. In every one of these, the pattern is the same: sides with partly shared and partly opposed interests talk until they reach an agreement.

collegeVersion.heading: Positions versus interests
collegeVersion.body: In any negotiation, each side says what it wants; that is its position. The underlying need the demand serves is its interest. Getting to Yes teaches negotiators to explore the interests underneath stated positions, because positions collide while interests can often both be satisfied. Original example: Sasha and Jordan share an apartment. Sasha insists the bedroom window stay open all night — her position. Jordan insists it stay shut — his position. The interests underneath: Sasha cannot sleep in a stuffy room, and Jordan is kept awake by street noise and pollen. Once the positions are set aside, the fix is easy: keep the window closed but run a fan in Sasha's corner and move her bed away from the wall. Both needs are met, even though the positions looked opposite. The lesson: when a negotiation stalls on demands, ask what each demand is really protecting.

collegeVersion.heading: Distributive versus integrative
collegeVersion.body: CFI sorts negotiations into two broad kinds. Distributive negotiation is hard bargaining over a fixed amount: any gain for one side is a loss for the other, like two food trucks competing for the single last parking spot at a festival — one parks, the other does not. Integrative negotiation looks for ways to create value so that both sides can come out ahead; CFI describes it as aiming for a win-win situation. Same festival, different approach: the two trucks agree to share the spot on alternate hours and split the crowd's business. The first kind divides a fixed pie; the second tries to grow the pie. Most real negotiations contain both flavors, and noticing which one you are in — or could move toward — is a large part of negotiating skill.

collegeVersion.heading: Prepare: target, walk-away, and the other side
collegeVersion.body: CFI's advice is to assess what you are seeking and what the other party is seeking before the talk begins. Add one more number: your walk-away. Fisher, Ury, and Patton call it your BATNA — your best alternative to a negotiated agreement — and the Program on Negotiation calls a strong BATNA the negotiator's greatest source of power. Before negotiating, figure out your target (the outcome you are aiming for), your walk-away (the point below which you take your alternative instead), and what the other side needs (so you know what they can give). Job hunters who keep following other leads and buyers who talk to a seller's competitors are improving their alternatives, which quietly strengthens their hand.

collegeVersion.heading: A simple process: open, explore, propose, agree
collegeVersion.body: Negotiations need no elaborate ritual. A plain four-step flow — open, explore, propose, agree — carries most of them, and it echoes the general process CFI describes: discussion, clarification, negotiating an outcome, and agreement. Open: start the conversation and set a cooperative tone. Explore: ask questions and learn what each side actually needs. Propose: offer a concrete deal, and be ready to adjust it. Agree: confirm the terms clearly enough that both sides know what they committed to. Skipping a step — proposing before exploring, or agreeing without confirming — is where deals go wrong.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The best deal is one both sides can live with. CFI warns that a negotiator who only cares about winning creates hostility and is less likely to keep the outcome, and the U.S. Office of Personnel Management defines the negotiating competency, in part, as building consensus through give and take. A deal that crushes one side tends to unravel later — the resentful party stops honoring it, and everyone loses. A durable agreement is not the one that maximized your take; it is the one that leaves both sides able to say yes and mean it.

vocabulary.definition: A discussion between two or more sides aimed at reaching an agreement, where each side has some interests it shares with the other and some it opposes.
What a side says it wants in a negotiation — its stated demand, such as a specific price or a delivery date.
The underlying need, worry, or goal that a position is meant to protect or satisfy.
Bargaining over a fixed amount of value, where any gain for one side is a loss for the other.
Bargaining that looks for ways to create additional value so both sides can come out ahead.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement; the fallback you can take if talks fail, and the floor beneath your walk-away point.
The least favorable deal you will accept before choosing your alternative instead.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Negotiation is talking to find a deal you can both accept. You do it more than you think: agreeing on a price, a deadline, or who cooks dinner is all negotiation. The key move is to look underneath the demands. Your position is what you say you want; your interest is why you want it. Two people who argue over positions often find they actually need the same thing. And before you talk, know your walk-away: what you will do if no deal happens. That knowledge is quiet power. The goal is not to crush the other side; a deal they cannot live with tends to collapse later. Aim for an agreement both of you can keep.
eli10.analogy: Think of a pizza. In a distributive negotiation, there is one pizza and you are arguing over the slices: every slice you take is a slice they lose. In an integrative negotiation, you look for ways to make the deal better for both — order a bigger pizza, or agree on toppings you both like. The first splits a fixed pie; the second grows it.
eli10.analogyLimits: A pizza has one price and one size, so growing the pie is easy to picture. Real negotiations are messier: value is subjective, information is incomplete, and the relationship matters as much as the slices. Sometimes the pie genuinely cannot grow — budgets and deadlines are real limits — and then you are back to dividing it fairly. And unlike a pizza order, people carry emotions and history into the room, so the numbers are never the whole story.

workedExample: Maya runs a small catering business and needs a used delivery van. Her target is $8,000; her walk-away is $9,500, because above that she will keep using her old van and borrow her cousin's van — her BATNA. Before meeting the seller, she learns he is moving abroad in three weeks and must sell fast, and that his interest is a quick, sure sale, not top dollar. Her position is eight thousand; his is ten thousand. Instead of haggling the gap, she explores: he needs speed, she needs a working van with a clean title. They agree at $8,600 with payment in full that week and a mechanic's inspection the same day — she stays under her walk-away, and he gets the fast, certain sale he needs. Both sides can live with the deal, which is the test of a good one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Digging in on your position — my price or nothing — and treating the other side's demand as the enemy.
commonMistakes.correction: A position is just the surface. Ask what need your demand and their demand are each protecting; interests can often both be satisfied.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating every negotiation as a fixed pie, assuming your gain must be their loss.
commonMistakes.correction: Check for integrative moves first — different priorities can create value for both sides. If the pie is truly fixed, then divide it, but know you are in a distributive negotiation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Walking in without a walk-away point, then accepting a bad deal out of fear of losing the conversation.
commonMistakes.correction: Name your BATNA before you start. Knowing your fallback tells you when to accept and when to walk.

commonMistakes.mistake: Celebrating a one-sided win and calling the negotiation over.
commonMistakes.correction: A deal the other side cannot live with tends to fall apart later — they stop honoring it, and the win evaporates. Aim for terms both sides can keep.

compareContrast.distinction: A position is what a side says it wants; the interest is the underlying need the demand protects. Two opposite positions — window open versus window shut — can sit on top of interests that are both satisfiable.
Distributive bargaining divides a fixed pie, so one side's gain is the other's loss; integrative bargaining tries to grow the pie so both sides can win. Real negotiations often mix the two.

Negotiation is the give-and-take of reaching an agreement between sides with partly shared and partly opposed interests; conflict resolution is the broader field of settling disagreements peacefully, of which negotiation is one tool (covered in its own lesson).

keyTakeaway: Negotiation is the give-and-take of reaching an agreement: prepare a target and a walk-away, look for the interests beneath the positions, and aim for a deal both sides can live with.

questionBank.prompt: Two project leads are trading proposals over who owns which launch-week tasks, and both expect to finish with a split they can accept. Their back-and-forth is negotiation, which the Program on Negotiation, quoting Getting to Yes, describes as —
options: Back-and-forth communication designed to reach an agreement when the sides share some interests and oppose others
A formal vote in which the majority's choice binds everyone
A one-sided decision handed down by whoever holds more authority
A private conversation with no goal beyond exchanging information
questionBank.explanation: The Getting to Yes definition, quoted by the Program on Negotiation, describes negotiation as back-and-forth communication designed to reach an agreement when the sides have some shared and some opposed interests. A vote, a command, and a goal-free chat each miss the give-and-take toward agreement.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attributed working definition of negotiation

questionBank.prompt: A bakery owner tells the delivery driver that every order must arrive by 6 a.m. sharp. The driver's real worry is that morning traffic will rattle the fragile pastry boxes, so she asks to load the van the night before. In this negotiation, the driver's interest is —
options: Protecting the fragile pastries from traffic damage
questionBank.explanation: An interest is the underlying need behind a position. The driver's need is that the pastries arrive undamaged; the 6 a.m. time is the bakery's stated demand. Loading the van the night before meets both the driver's interest and the bakery's deadline.
questionBank.skill: Applying the positions-versus-interests distinction to a delivery dispute

questionBank.prompt: Two food trucks want the last parking spot at a festival. The organizer tells them whoever pays the higher fee gets it — one wins the spot, the other drives away. This fixed-pie arrangement is an example of —
questionBank.explanation: CFI describes distributive negotiation as hard bargaining over a fixed amount: any gain for one side comes at the other's expense, as when one truck's win is the other's loss. Integrative negotiation would look for a way both trucks could benefit, such as sharing the spot.
questionBank.skill: Identifying distributive negotiation in a fixed-pie scenario

questionBank.prompt: Before meeting the seller, Nina lines up a second client who will pay her usual rate if the current deal falls through. The second client is Nina's —
options: BATNA — her best alternative to a negotiated agreement
questionBank.explanation: A BATNA is the best alternative to a negotiated agreement — what you will do if talks fail. Fisher, Ury, and Patton call a strong BATNA a negotiator's greatest source of power. Nina's second client is her fallback, not her position or her target.
questionBank.skill: Applying the BATNA concept to a preparation scenario

questionBank.prompt: Two neighbors split the cost of a shared fence, and one negotiates hard enough to make the other pay for everything. The loser stops maintaining their side, and within two years the fence rots and must be replaced — costing both neighbors more than the original deal. What does this outcome show?
options: The best deal is one both sides can live with, because a resentful loser quietly undermines it
Hard bargaining is always the most efficient way to settle a fence dispute
Fence maintenance is a separate conflict and cannot be negotiated
A one-sided win is the sign of a well-negotiated agreement
questionBank.explanation: CFI warns that a negotiator who only takes and never gives creates hostility and is less likely to keep the outcome, and OPM frames negotiating as building consensus through give and take. The fence collapsed because one side could not live with the deal — durable agreements need both sides able to say yes and mean it.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why a one-sided deal fails the both-sides-can-live-with test

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources: Program on Negotiation (Harvard Law School) and CFI web pages read live on 2026-08-22 and paraphrased in original prose, with the one-sentence Getting to Yes working definition quoted with attribution; OPM's Guide to the Senior Executive Service Qualifications is a U.S. government work (public domain), read via a Wayback Machine capture (2025-11-11) because the current OPM ECQ page uses the revised 2023 framework that no longer lists the Influencing/Negotiating competency; no other source prose reproduced; all examples original.
provenance.transformation: Working definition (negotiation as a discussion aimed at reaching an agreement) synthesized from the Fisher, Ury, and Patton definition quoted by the Program on Negotiation and CFI's dialogue definition; the when-it-happens list (salaries, contracts, conflicts, purchases) follows PON's account of everyday negotiation settings; the positions-versus-interests distinction follows Getting to Yes as presented by PON (explore the interests underlying stated positions); the distributive-versus-integrative distinction follows CFI's forms of negotiation (fixed-pie hard bargaining versus win-win value creation); the preparation practice (target, walk-away/BATNA, know the other side) synthesized from PON's BATNA article and CFI's preparation guidance; the four-step process (open, explore, propose, agree) is a plain-language restatement of the general process CFI describes (discussion, clarification, negotiating an outcome, agreement); the honest framing (the best deal is one both sides can live with) built from CFI's hostility warning and OPM's give-and-take competency definition; the negotiation-as-management-competency claim from OPM's Guide to the SES Qualifications. All businesses, people, and scenarios (Sasha and Jordan's window, the festival food trucks, Maya's van, Nina's second client, the fence neighbors) are original.
